summary: For children aged 7-9, build the rule 'like poles repel, opposite poles attract' from repeated predict-then-test trials with two labelled magnets. The target is a predictive rule grounded in observation: every magnet has two poles (north-seeking/south-seeking); predict whether two magnets attract or repel from how their poles face. No field model or explanation of why yet. Repulsion of like poles is grasped more slowly than attraction of opposites, so give plentiful like-pole trials. Poles are a property of every magnet, whatever its shape.
misconceptions: Children are slow to adopt the idea of poles and only gradually come to see magnetic effects as attraction of unlike poles and repulsion of like poles (IOP Spark) — repulsion is grasped later than attraction.
Reversing the rule (thinking like poles attract) — hence the need for many disconfirming like-pole trials.
Thinking poles are always 'the two ends' — not true for ring/button magnets; poles are a property of every magnet whatever its shape.
Thinking any two magnets always just 'stick' — ignoring that orientation determines attract vs repel.
Assuming a bigger magnet is automatically the stronger one (carried over from the materials topic).

activities.title: Predict-then-test with two labelled magnets
steps: Take two bar magnets with poles colour-coded and labelled (e.g. north red, south blue).
Set an orientation by bringing two ends toward each other; before pushing, say aloud your prediction: will they attract or repel?
Slowly push them together and observe/feel what happens: do they snap together, or meet an invisible springy resistance that pushes them apart unless you force them?
Work through all four orientations: N-N, S-S, N-S, S-N. Record each in a table: draw the orientation, write your prediction, write what actually happened.
On one pair that repels (e.g. N-N), flip just ONE magnet and push again — notice the outcome reverses.
After enough trials, state the pattern you discovered in your own short rule.
activities.insight: Whether two magnets attract or repel depends on which poles face each other: like poles push apart, opposite poles pull together. Because flipping one magnet reverses the outcome with the SAME pair, the result depends on which poles face each other, not on which particular magnets you use.

activities.title: Confront the repulsion case head-on
steps: Spend extra trials on like-pole orientations (N-N and S-S), slowly pushing and feeling the resistance.
Describe the sensation: an invisible springy wall that slides and bounces and pushes the ends apart unless you force them together.
Predict the like-pole outcome ahead of each push, then test, until you reliably expect repulsion.
activities.insight: Two magnets can push each other away. Repulsion is just as real as attraction and happens specifically when like poles face.

activities.title: Poles on magnets of every shape
steps: Examine magnets of different shapes: bar, ring, button, horseshoe.

For a horseshoe or ring magnet, find where the poles are using iron filings (they cluster at the poles but cannot tell you which is north and which is south), then test with a labelled magnet to name each pole: the part that repels the labelled north pole is a north pole. Ring and button magnets often have their poles on the flat faces rather than at the ends.
State where the north and south poles are on each magnet — not just on the two ends of a bar.
activities.insight: Every magnet has a north and a south pole whatever its shape; poles are a property of the whole magnet, not simply 'the two ends of a bar'.

activities.title: Name the poles: the north-seeking anchor
steps: Let a single magnet turn freely: suspend it on a thread, or rest it on a small float (e.g. a cork or foam disc) on water, and watch it swing until it settles.
Keeping it away from other magnets and steel objects, notice which end points roughly north; name that end the 'north-seeking' pole and the other the 'south-seeking' pole.
Use this precise language ('north-seeking'/'south-seeking', progressing to 'north pole'/'south pole') when describing your predict-then-test trials.
activities.insight: A freely-moving magnet's north-seeking pole points north, which is where the name comes from. Consistent pole language keeps orientation unambiguous.

activities.title: Retrieval practice: predict the outcome
steps: Given a diagram of two magnets in a stated orientation (e.g. 'north facing north'), decide: attract or repel?
Match orientation diagrams to their outcomes.
Sort a set of orientations into two groups: those that attract and those that repel.
Answer transfer items: 'If a magnet is flipped, what changes?' and 'Where are the poles on this horseshoe?'
activities.insight: The rule can be applied reliably to new orientations, including the slower-learned like-pole (repel) cases and flipped magnets.

checkQuestion: I have two bar magnets. I turn them so their two RED (north) ends face each other and slowly push them together. What will happen as they get close — and why?
checkAnswer: They push apart / you feel them resist — they repel. Two like poles (north and north) repel each other; only opposite poles (north and south) attract. So facing two norths together makes them push away.
